html:
The Dawes Act of 1887 divided the communal lands of Native American reservations into private plots, usually 160 acres for each family head. Its aim was to turn Native people into farmers and citizens and to end tribal life.

Land left over after the plots were assigned was declared surplus and sold to white settlers. Many Native owners, unused to private titles and pressed by debt and fraud, lost their plots too.

Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934, when the Indian Reorganization Act ended allotment. In Indian Territory it opened the way for the land runs into Oklahoma. It worked alongside boarding schools and the loss of the bison, and Canada's Indian Act pursued similar ends.
